sheet.howExamined: Unit 2, one hour, fifty marks, six questions, calculator allowed, formula sheet on page 2. Vectors open the paper, as Question 1 or 2. Summer 2024 Q2 and Summer 2025 Q2 were 5 + 3 + 2: unknowns from a vector equation, the magnitude of a new resultant, then its direction. Summer 2023 Q1 was 2 + 2 + 2: an acceleration in vector form, a displacement vector and a missing force. Summer 2026 Q1 was the resultant of three forces, its magnitude (4 marks) and its angle with the horizontal (2). The Summer 2021 paper gave a resultant's magnitude and asked for both possible values of an unknown component. Schemes are written in MW and W, one mark per gathered coefficient, with follow-through applied throughout.

i and j left inside the scalar equations (Summer 2024 Q2(i))

Vectors subtracted or multiplied where they should be added (Summer 2022 Q2(i))
A magnitude or an angle given where a vector answer was asked for (Summer 2023 Q1)

A velocity given where the speed was asked for (Summer 2019 Q2(ii))

Turn one vector equation into two scalar equations, and solve them.

noteBlocks.md: A vector in $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ form is two numbers under one name: how far across and how far up. Adding two vectors means walking one and then the other, nose to tail. The single arrow from start to finish is the sum, and its components are the totals of the two columns: the $\mathbf{i}$ terms together, the $\mathbf{j}$ terms together. Subtracting works the same way, one column at a time.

noteBlocks.stem: Two forces, $(7\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j})$ N and $(-3\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j})$ N, act on a body. Find their resultant.

steps.decision: The resultant is the sum of the forces. The sum written out with its brackets is the method mark.
Total each column on its own. Adding a negative component takes it away.
Put the two totals back together as one vector: the answer keeps its i and its j.

noteBlocks.prompt: Two forces, $(5\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j})$ N and $(-8\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j})$ N, act on a body. What is the $\mathbf{i}$ component of their resultant, in newtons?
noteBlocks.explain: Total the $\mathbf{i}$ column on its own, as in step 2 of See it: $5 + (-8) = -3$. The $\mathbf{j}$ terms never enter it; they total 7 in their own column.

twin.prompt: Two forces, $(2\mathbf{i} - 9\mathbf{j})$ N and $(6\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j})$ N, act on a body. What is the $\mathbf{j}$ component of their resultant, in newtons?

noteBlocks.caption: Tripling the arrow triples both components. Tripling only one swings the arrow round.

noteBlocks.md:
Multiplying a vector by a number stretches the arrow, so every component is multiplied, sign included. Leave one alone and the arrow turns as well as stretching.

For a combination such as $3\mathbf{a} - 2\mathbf{b}$, scale each vector on its own line first, with brackets, then combine column by column. Subtracting a negative component adds to the total.

noteBlocks.title: Why the scalar cannot skip a component
noteBlocks.md: An arrow's direction is set by how far up it goes for each step across. Triple both and that rate stays the same, so the arrow only gets longer. Triple one alone and the rate changes, so the arrow points somewhere new.

steps.decision: The 3 multiplies both components, so $-3\mathbf{j}$ becomes $-9\mathbf{j}$.
The same for $\mathbf{b}$, on its own line, before anything is combined.
Subtract column by column. Taking away −4 adds 4, and that is where the sign most often goes.

noteBlocks.prompt: $\mathbf{a} = (2\mathbf{i} - 5\mathbf{j})$ and $\mathbf{b} = (3\mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j})$. What is the $\mathbf{j}$ component of $2\mathbf{a} - 3\mathbf{b}$?
noteBlocks.explain: Scale first, as in steps 1 and 2 of See it: $2\mathbf{a}$ has $-10\mathbf{j}$ and $3\mathbf{b}$ has $-12\mathbf{j}$. Then $-10 - (-12) = 2$: taking away a negative adds.

twin.prompt: $\mathbf{a} = (\mathbf{i} - 6\mathbf{j})$ and $\mathbf{b} = (4\mathbf{i} - 5\mathbf{j})$. What is the $\mathbf{j}$ component of $3\mathbf{a} - 2\mathbf{b}$?

noteBlocks.text: Why one vector equation is two

noteBlocks.md: $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ are at right angles, so no amount of $\mathbf{i}$ can ever make any $\mathbf{j}$: a step east never moves you north. That is why the columns never mix, and it has a second use. When two vectors are equal, their $\mathbf{i}$ parts must match and their $\mathbf{j}$ parts must match. One vector equation carries two ordinary equations, exactly enough for two unknowns.

noteBlocks.stem: Show that if $a\mathbf{i} + b\mathbf{j} = c\mathbf{i} + d\mathbf{j}$, then $a = c$ and $b = d$.

steps.decision: Gather the $\mathbf{i}$ terms on the left and the $\mathbf{j}$ terms on the right.

steps.working: The left side points along the x-axis; the right side points along the y-axis
steps.decision: A number times $\mathbf{i}$ is an arrow across and a number times $\mathbf{j}$ is an arrow up, at right angles to it.
Two arrows at right angles can only be equal if neither goes anywhere: both have zero length.
Equal vectors: the $\mathbf{i}$ parts equal and the $\mathbf{j}$ parts equal. Two equations, one from each direction.

noteBlocks.explain: The $\mathbf{i}$ parts are equated with each other and the $\mathbf{j}$ parts with each other, as in step 4 of See it: two equations, so $p = 7$ and $q = 5$.

optionNotes.why: One equation from everything mixes the directions; each direction gives its own.
The i part is paired with the j part here, where i must match i and j must match j.
Adding everything into one equation mixes the two directions, which are at right angles, so each direction gives an equation of its own.
This pairs each number with the one next to it on the page, not with its own direction: i goes with i, and j with j.

noteBlocks.md: The paper's five-mark part gives vectors with letters in them and an equation they satisfy. The route never changes: substitute with a bracket round every vector, expand every bracket, then write one line for the $\mathbf{i}$ terms and one for the $\mathbf{j}$ terms. Drop the $\mathbf{i}$ and the $\mathbf{j}$ at that point; what is left is a pair of simultaneous equations.

noteBlocks.title: Summer 2024 and 2025, Question 2(i)
noteBlocks.md: Most candidates substituted and then stopped: few equated the $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ coefficients, and many left $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ inside their equations. In 2025 the sign of $-3 \times -3x$ was the slip.

noteBlocks.stem: Forces $\mathbf{P} = (x\mathbf{i} + y\mathbf{j})$ N and $\mathbf{Q} = (2y\mathbf{i} - x\mathbf{j})$ N satisfy $4\mathbf{P} - 3\mathbf{Q} = (32\mathbf{i} + 7\mathbf{j})$ N. Find $x$ and $y$.

steps.decision: Substitute with a bracket round each vector, so the 4 and the $-3$ reach every term.
Expand. $-3 \times -x\mathbf{j}$ is $+3x\mathbf{j}$: two negatives make a plus.
Gather the $\mathbf{i}$ terms and equate them. The $\mathbf{i}$ has done its job and is dropped.
The same for the $\mathbf{j}$ terms: two ordinary equations, no $\mathbf{i}$ or $\mathbf{j}$ in either.
Eliminate, solve, then check both values in the equation you did not use: $3(5) + 4(-2) = 7$.

noteBlocks.title: Vectors Using i and j notation
noteBlocks.why: The same arithmetic at a slower pace, with every bracket written out. Watch the i line and the j line being kept apart.

noteBlocks.prompt: $(x\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j}) - 2(\mathbf{i} - y\mathbf{j}) = 5\mathbf{i} + 13\mathbf{j}$. What is the value of $y$?
noteBlocks.explain: Expand first, as in step 2 of See it: $-2 \times -y\mathbf{j} = +2y\mathbf{j}$. The $\mathbf{j}$ line is $3 + 2y = 13$, so $y = 5$. Writing $-2y$ would give $-5$.

twin.prompt: $(4\mathbf{i} + y\mathbf{j}) - 3(x\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j}) = -5\mathbf{i} + 10\mathbf{j}$. What is the value of $y$?

noteBlocks.caption: Straight from A to B, or back to O and out again: the same journey.

noteBlocks.md: A position vector runs from the origin $O$ to a point: $\mathbf{a}$ is $\overrightarrow{OA}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ is $\overrightarrow{OB}$. The displacement from $A$ to $B$ is the arrow straight between them. Going there directly, or going round by $O$, ends in the same place, and that one fact gives the rule.

noteBlocks.stem: Show that the displacement from $A$ to $B$ is $\overrightarrow{AB} = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a}$.

steps.decision: From $O$, going to $A$ and then on to $B$ lands where going straight to $B$ does.
The two arrows from $O$ are the position vectors.
Take $\mathbf{a}$ from both sides: the finish's position vector minus the start's.

noteBlocks.prompt: $P$ has position vector $\mathbf{p}$ and $Q$ has position vector $\mathbf{q}$. What is $\overrightarrow{QP}$, the displacement from $Q$ to $P$?
noteBlocks.explain: The journey starts at $Q$ and finishes at $P$, so it is the finish minus the start, as step 3 of See it shows.

twin.prompt: $C$ has position vector $\mathbf{c}$ and $D$ has position vector $\mathbf{d}$. What is $\overrightarrow{CD}$?
twin.explain: From $C$ to $D$: the finish, $\mathbf{d}$, minus the start, $\mathbf{c}$.

optionNotes.why: That is the journey from D back to C, because the finish comes first.
Adding position vectors lands somewhere else entirely; the displacement is a difference.
That is the journey from P to Q: the same arrow, pointing back the other way.
Adding the position vectors lands at a point that is neither P nor Q, whereas a displacement between two points takes one from the other.

noteBlocks.text: Displacement and distance between two points

noteBlocks.md: With numbers in, find $\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a}$ one column at a time, with a bracket round each position vector so the minus reaches both components. That answer is a vector. If the question asks how far apart the points are, the distance is its magnitude, a single number, found as in the magnitude topic.

noteBlocks.stem: $P$ has position vector $(-3\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j})$ m and $Q$ has position vector $(5\mathbf{i} - 10\mathbf{j})$ m. Find $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ and the distance $PQ$.

steps.decision: Finish minus start, with a bracket round each.
$5 - (-3) = 8$ and $-10 - 5 = -15$. This part asks for a vector, so both components stay.
A distance is a length: the magnitude of the displacement. Squaring removes the minus sign.

noteBlocks.prompt: $A$ has position vector $(3\mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j})$ m and $B$ has position vector $(-2\mathbf{i} + 8\mathbf{j})$ m. What is the $\mathbf{j}$ component of $\overrightarrow{AB}$, in metres?
noteBlocks.explain: Finish minus start, one column at a time, as in step 2 of See it: $8 - (-4) = 12$. Taking away −4 adds 4; $-4 - 8 = -12$ would be the journey back.

twin.prompt: $C$ has position vector $(-\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j})$ m and $D$ has position vector $(5\mathbf{i} - 7\mathbf{j})$ m. What is the $\mathbf{i}$ component of $\overrightarrow{CD}$, in metres?

noteBlocks.md: $\mathbf{F} = m\mathbf{a}$, $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{a}t$ and $\mathbf{s} = \mathbf{u}t + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}t^2$ work exactly as they do with numbers, one component at a time. The mass and the time stay plain numbers: dividing a force vector by the mass divides both of its components, and $t^2$ multiplies both components of $\mathbf{a}$.

noteBlocks.stem: A particle of mass 2 kg has initial velocity $(4\mathbf{i} - 7\mathbf{j})$ m/s. A constant force $(6\mathbf{i} + 10\mathbf{j})$ N acts on it. Find its acceleration, then its displacement after 2 seconds.

steps.decision: $\mathbf{F} = m\mathbf{a}$ with the numbers in: this line earns the method mark.
Divide both components by the mass.
$\mathbf{s} = \mathbf{u}t + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}t^2$ with $t = 2$; square the time before it multiplies.
Work each term out, then add the columns.

noteBlocks.prompt: A particle has initial velocity $(\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j})$ m/s and constant acceleration $(2\mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j})$ m/s². What is the $\mathbf{j}$ component of its displacement after 3 seconds, in metres?

That adds the components to make 5, but a magnitude squares, adds and roots them: (x + 3)² + 4² = 5².

noteBlocks.stem: The force $\mathbf{F} = (2\mathbf{i} - 5\mathbf{j})$ N is the resultant of three forces. Two of them are $(6\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j})$ N and $(-3\mathbf{i} - 8\mathbf{j})$ N. Find the third force.

steps.decision: Substitute with a bracket round every vector. The brackets are what carry the $-2$ to both terms of $\mathbf{f}$.

options.feedback: Every vector in its bracket, so each scalar reaches every term.
Without brackets the 3 and the −2 reach only the first term of each vector.
The equation takes 2f away; adding it changes every term that comes from f.

steps.decision: Expand every bracket. $-2 \times -3x\mathbf{j}$ is $+6x\mathbf{j}$: two negatives make a plus.

options: Because a negative times a negative is positive, so the −2 turns −3xj into +6xj
Because the minus sign in front of f changes only its i term
Because the j terms of an expansion always come out positive
whyMenu.explain: The −2 multiplies every term inside the bracket, and −2 × −3x is +6x. This is the sign the Summer 2025 report saw going wrong.

options.feedback: Both brackets expanded, the sign of the last term included.

The −2 has reached only the first term of f; it multiplies the −3xj too.

steps.decision: One vector equation is two ordinary ones. Gather the $\mathbf{i}$ terms, then drop the $\mathbf{i}$: it has done its job.

Equal vectors have equal i parts and equal j parts: two separate equations.

parts.stem:
Throughout this question, $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ are perpendicular unit vectors, $\mathbf{i}$ along the x-axis and $\mathbf{j}$ along the y-axis, with displacement in metres and time in seconds.

A body starts at the point with position vector $(2\mathbf{i} + 9\mathbf{j})$ m and moves with constant velocity $(8\mathbf{i} - 6\mathbf{j})$ m/s.

Find its position vector after 5 seconds.

Answer ________ m
hints: Constant velocity means the displacement is the velocity times the time.
Add that displacement to where the body started.
parts.workedSolution: The displacement is $5(8\mathbf{i} - 6\mathbf{j}) = 40\mathbf{i} - 30\mathbf{j}$ m, so the position vector becomes $(2\mathbf{i} + 9\mathbf{j}) + (40\mathbf{i} - 30\mathbf{j}) = 42\mathbf{i} - 21\mathbf{j}$ m.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the displacement over the 5 seconds, which earns both method marks (M). The body did not start at the origin, so the starting position vector still has to be added on.
The velocity has been added once, as if the body moved for 1 second. The method marks need the displacement as 5 times the velocity; then add it to the start.

parts.stem:
Find the displacement of the body from its starting point over the 5 seconds.

Answer ________ m

scheme.for: $5\mathbf{v}$, or the position vector after 5 s minus the starting one

hints: Displacement is the finish minus the start.
It is also simply the velocity times the time here.
parts.workedSolution: $(42\mathbf{i} - 21\mathbf{j}) - (2\mathbf{i} + 9\mathbf{j}) = 40\mathbf{i} - 30\mathbf{j}$ m, which is the same as $5(8\mathbf{i} - 6\mathbf{j})$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is where the body finished, not how far it moved. A displacement is the finish's position vector minus the start's.

parts.stem:
Calculate the distance the body travels in the 5 seconds.

Answer ________ m
hints: The path is straight, so the distance is the magnitude of the displacement.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the sum of the squares. The substitution earns the method mark (M); the square root is the step that gives a length.
That adds the two components. The body travels straight along the arrow, not across and then down.

questions.solutionProgram: start = 2i + 9j; v = 8i - 6j; t = 5; disp = t*v = 40i - 30j; end = start + disp = 42i - 21j; distance = 50

findTheMistake.stem: Niamh is finding the resultant of two forces $(6\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j})$ N and $(-5\mathbf{i} + 9\mathbf{j})$ N. Her working:
studentWorking: Resultant = the vector sum of the forces
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 3 subtracts the second force's $\mathbf{j}$ component where line 1 says the forces are added. The $\mathbf{i}$ line is right: -5 is already negative, so adding it takes 5 away and gives 1. The $\mathbf{j}$ line should add 9 to -2 and give 7.
correction: Resultant = the vector sum of the forces
findTheMistake.feedback: Naming the resultant as the vector sum and keeping the two columns apart is the method, and it earns the method mark (M). One operation applies to the whole vector, so if the i line adds, the j line adds too. Writing the two vectors one above the other before you start makes a stray sign very hard to miss.

findTheMistake.stem: Dara is solving $x\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j} = 8\mathbf{i} + y\mathbf{j}$ for $x$ and $y$. His working:
studentWorking: Two vectors are equal, so their components match
x i + 5 j - 8 i - y j = 0
x i - 8 i = 0 and 5 j - y j = 0, so x i = 8 i and 5 j = y j
x i = 8 i, so x = 8 i and y = 5 j
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 4 keeps the $\mathbf{i}$ and the $\mathbf{j}$ inside the answers. Once the terms have been gathered, the letters have done their job of saying which terms belong together: what is left is a pair of ordinary scalar equations, so the answers are $x = 8$ and $y = 5$ with no $\mathbf{i}$ or $\mathbf{j}$ attached.
correction: Two vectors are equal, so their components match
findTheMistake.feedback: The reasoning is right the whole way down, and equating the two pairs of coefficients earns the method marks (M). $x$ is a number of newtons, or metres, and a number never carries an $\mathbf{i}$. Examiners report this every year, so it is worth one last look before the answer line.

findTheMistake.stem: Tomás is working out $2\mathbf{p} - 3\mathbf{q}$, where $\mathbf{p} = (3\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j})$ and $\mathbf{q} = (-2\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j})$. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 3 adds the $\mathbf{i}$ component of $3\mathbf{q}$ where the question subtracts it. That component is -6, so adding it takes 6 away and the line comes out as 0. Subtracting a negative adds, so the line should read 6 - (-6) = 12.
findTheMistake.feedback: Scaling both vectors first is exactly right and earns both method marks (M). The habit that saves the sign is writing the subtraction out with the bracket in place before any arithmetic happens, so a negative inside a bracket is visible when the minus outside it arrives.

prompts.prompt: A part asks for a resultant in vector form. What must the answer keep?
prompts.answer: Both components, so it is written in i and j form rather than reduced to a magnitude.

prompts.prompt: What is the first line to write in a vector equation with unknowns?
prompts.answer: The substitution with brackets round every vector, so the scalar outside reaches every term inside.

prompts.prompt: How do you add two vectors given in i and j form?
prompts.answer: Add the i parts together and the j parts together.

prompts.prompt: Using position vectors, how do you find the displacement from A to B?
prompts.answer: b − a: the position vector of B minus that of A.

prompts.prompt: How do F = ma and v = u + at work with vectors?
prompts.answer: One component at a time; the mass and the time stay numbers.

prompts.prompt: What does multiplying a vector by a number do to its components?
prompts.answer: It multiplies every component, sign included.

prompts.prompt: Two vectors in i and j form are equal. What do you equate?
prompts.answer: The i parts with each other, then the j parts: two equations.

findings.asked: Vector calculations including a displacement vector.
findings.wentWrong: Magnitudes and angles were produced where vectors were asked; the displacement vector was not formed; sign handling failed in the last part.

findings.asked: Substitute vectors into an equation and find unknowns; magnitude.
findings.wentWrong: Few got beyond substituting: equating the i coefficients and the j coefficients to make simultaneous equations was rare; i and j were left in the equations; sign errors in expansions.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Collected i terms and j terms, set each equal, solved the pair.
findings.rule: Equal vectors: equal i parts AND equal j parts.

findings.asked: Vector equation with unknowns; magnitude; direction.
findings.wentWrong: -3 times -3x mis-signed; the simultaneous equations solved wrongly even by strong candidates; i and j dropped mid-working; the direction used the reciprocal ratio.
findings.rule: tan of the angle = j component over i component (check which axis the angle is measured from).

findings.asked: Vector and scalar definitions with examples.
findings.wentWrong: Under half full marks; weight was frequently called a scalar.
findings.rule: Weight is a force, so a vector; mass is a scalar.

findings.wentWrong: Definitions unknown or swapped; specific examples offered as definitions.
findings.rule: Vector: magnitude and direction; scalar: magnitude only - then give an example.

insight.ruleToRemember: Keep i and j components separate; equal vectors give two scalar equations; magnitude = root of the sum of squares; direction from tan = j/i measured from the correct axis; speed is the magnitude of velocity.
insight.aStarSignal: Turning a vector equation with unknowns into simultaneous equations and finishing with a direction angle measured correctly.
